extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in media studies, political science, and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria about news production, truth, propaganda, and the formation of public opinion as presented in Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion (1922). Useful for analyzing how media selection, economics, and psychology shape public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment / subjective mental image
rubrics_metrics.description: "The real environment is altogether too big, too complex, and too fleeting for direct acquaintance... Instead, people construct a pseudo-environment that is a subjective, biased, and necessarily abridged mental image of the world, and to a degree, everyone's pseudo-environment is a fiction. People 'live in the same world, but they think and feel in different ones.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a cognitive limitation that any evaluation of public opinion or news must account for: individuals act on their constructed pseudo-environments, not on the full 'real environment.' Consequence: analyses should consider how simplified stereotypes and mental images mediate perception and behavior. (Related term: social constructionism/constructed reality.)

rubrics_metrics.name: News and truth are necessarily incomplete and arranged
rubrics_metrics.description: "By definition, pertinent facts are never provided completely and accurately; by necessity they are arranged to portray a certain, subjective interpretation of an event."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat news as an arranged selection of facts rather than a complete representation. The page notes that those most familiar with facts will construct pseudo-environments aligned with their stereotypes and may convey selective interpretations to the public to suit private needs. When assessing news, look for what is omitted and how facts are framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda requires a barrier of censorship; media are vulnerable to manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Propaganda inherently requires a barrier of censorship between the event and the public. Thus mass communication media, by their nature as vehicles for informational transmission, are essentially vulnerable to manipulation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies censorship and information barriers as a necessary condition for propaganda. Evaluations should examine gatekeeping, censorship, and other barriers that permit manipulation. The text emphasizes that vulnerability is not solely technological but also social/intellectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic incentives shape media: the 'buying public' and the 'bewildered herd'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The buying public: the 'bewildered herd' ... must pay to understand the unseen environment by the mass communications media... People will be selective and will buy the most factual media at the lowest price."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the market constraint on access to information: media must balance social function (transmitting public affairs) and profit/survival. Criterion for judging media includes affordability, market incentives, and how these influence selection and presentation of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of news favors confirmed and official matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "People publish already-confirmed news that are thus less disputable. Officially-available public matters will constitute 'the news' and unofficial (private) matters are unavailable, are less available, or are used as 'issues' for propaganda."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests that news-making privileges officially-available, confirmed information; unofficial or private information is less likely to become news or may be instrumentalized. Use this to analyze why certain topics surface and others do not, and to spot potential propaganda uses of unofficial information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of news as signal shaped by editorial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "The function of news is to signal an event, and that signalling, eventually, is a consequence of editorial selection and judgement; journalism creates and sows the seeds (news) that establish public opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative focus should be on editorial judgement: selection, prominence, and framing decisions are central mechanisms by which news shapes public opinion. Assess editorial processes and choices when determining news reliability and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent: role and limits of expert, specialized class
rubrics_metrics.description: "When properly deployed in the public interest, the manufacture of consent is useful and necessary for a democratic society... [Lippmann] proposes that a professional, 'specialized class' collect and analyze data, and present their conclusions to the society's decision makers, who, in their turn, use the 'art of persuasion' to inform the public about the decisions and circumstances affecting them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents a normative claim that expertise and organized dissemination (manufacture of consent) may be necessary because most people cannot or will not do the complex analysis required. When applying this criterion, examine who the 'specialized' actors are, their accountability, and whether their persuasion serves public interest or narrow interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for verification and limits of intuition/intuition-based democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is no longer possible... that the knowledge needed for the management of human affairs comes up spontaneously from the human heart... we cannot rely upon intuition, conscience, or the accidents of casual opinion if we are to deal with the world beyond our reach."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that intuition and casual opinion are insufficient for complex public affairs; stresses the need for verified, critical analysis. Use this as a criterion to favor evidence-based reporting and to be skeptical of appeals to intuition or emotion without supporting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic alternative: inclusion of the public in discourse (Dewey's critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizes John Dewey's rejection of Lippmann's technocratic prescription: Dewey agreed the public is often irrational but rejected a technocratic elite, arguing that in a democracy the people are part of public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames an evaluative trade-off: whether media and public affairs processes should rely more on expert intermediaries or promote broader public participation. When judging practices, weigh inclusivity and democratic engagement versus efficiency/accuracy from specialized actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of management-of-opinion dynamics (Herman & Chomsky citation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lippmann's advocacy of 'manufacture of consent' is noted as referring 'to the management of public opinion, which Lippmann felt was necessary for democracy to flourish, since he felt that public opinion was an irrational force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls attention to the potential for deliberate management of public opinion. Use this to evaluate media systems for structural biases, ownership and power influences, and whether mechanisms exist that enable elite-driven 'management' rather than open deliberation.
